report:
### Research Summary

**Conclusion:** The claim that a vegetarian diet inherently increases total life expectancy compared to eating meat is only partially supported by scientific evidence. While vegetarianism is consistently associated with lower heart disease mortality, overall all-cause mortality rates between vegetarians and health-conscious meat eaters are largely comparable.

### Key Evidence

1. **Cardiovascular Benefits:** Meta-analyses show that vegetarians experience a statistically significant reduction in ischemic heart disease mortality compared to non-vegetarians (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/).
2. **Population-Specific Differences:** Long-term cohort studies of Seventh-day Adventists show longer life expectancy and reduced mortality among vegetarians (https://veganhealth.org/chronic-disease-and-vegetarian-diets/vegetarian-cohorts/). However, large general-population studies—such as Australia's 45 and Up Study—found no significant difference in all-cause mortality between vegetarians and regular meat-eaters after controlling for demographic and lifestyle factors (https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/items/c6ae4f02-92e6-40ea-98e0-3fd71cdcc133).
3. **Lifestyle Confounding Factors:** Studies indicate that vegetarians often engage in healthier overall habits, including lower smoking rates, higher physical activity, and lower alcohol intake. When non-vegetarians maintain similarly healthy habits, differences in overall longevity largely disappear, though high-quality plant-based diets remain strongly protective against cardiovascular disease (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2024.1481363/full).
